Paper topic: whether internal computations of in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Finds ICL and SFT activation patterns differ even when using same data. Proposed method: ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), trains a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations; then SFT trains this primed model on ground-truth responses. Experiments: 12 benchmarks, two model families, >13,000 trained models. Reported outcomes: improvements in SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT identify different weight subspaces. Caveat: IA2-based training does not consistently outperform ICL, especially on some multi-token math tasks. Also examines simultaneous IA2+SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method.

Paper studies whether internal computations of in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Defines IA2 / ICL Activation Alignment as self-distillation: train a model without demonstrations to match its own ICL-conditioned activations; “priming” = IA2 before SFT, written IA2 → SFT. IA2 + SFT means simultaneous activation-matching and SFT losses. SFT uses cross-entropy on ground-truth tokens; IA2 uses mean-squared/norm activation-matching loss. Activation similarity (asim) = token-wise cosine similarity, often layerwise. Main claim from earlier: ICL and SFT activation patterns differ even with same data; IA2 improves SFT accuracy/calibration on 12 benchmarks, two model families, >13k trained models, but does not consistently beat ICL, especially some multi-token math. IA2 and SFT weight updates are nearly orthogonal/different subspaces; subspace overlap formula = (1/r)||U1^T U2||_F^2 from SVD bases, LoRA rank r=8 main experiments. Models: Qwen3-4B-Base across tasks; Llama-3.2 family (1B/3B for single-token, 1B-Instruct for multi-token). Tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), news (AGNews, BBCNews), StrategyQA True/False, SciQ/QASC MCQ incl remapped SciQr/QASCr, GSM8K/GSM8Ks/HMathA math. Metrics: accuracy; ECE for single-token; multi-token parsed exact match/format. Training: N shots/samples, up to 50 epochs, learning rates 1e-4/3e-4/1e-3; hyperparameter selection by best performance. IA2 collects ICL activations for response tokens (shape L×G×d, G capped at 200), using N−1 demos per sample. Other comparisons: IA2 only, SFT only, simultaneous IA2+SFT with beta, soft-label/KD, alternative PEFT (IA3), full fine-tuning/LoRA target modules. Caveats/future: prompt optimization, selective IA2, LoRA ablations, catastrophic forgetting, RL-tuned models.

IA2 + SFT = simultaneous activation-matching and SFT losses. SFT cross-entropy over all generated response tokens. ICL prompt I=[X1∘Y1...Xn∘Yn]+query Xt, no weight updates. Activations A are L×R×d; asim(A1,A2)=token-wise cosine similarity, size L×R. §3 compares A_ICL with T=[I∘X] to A_SFT with T=X at output-token positions, averaged over tokens/samples/datasets; 100 test samples from datasets incl SST2, AGNews; models Qwen3 and Llama-3.2: 1B=16 layers, 3B=28, 4B=36. Claim: ICL and SFT activations not aligned; similarity better in initial/final layers, worse middle. Claim: ICL better calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy (Fig 1). Fig 2 “SFT only” has low asim with ICL; IA2→SFT aligns more and performs better. Table 1 examples: SST2→SST2 acc 65.2 vs 90.4, ECE 0.22 vs 0.06; FinS→FinS acc 67.4 vs 78.7, ECE 0.31 vs 0.16. Table 2 examples: SciQ→SciQ acc 35.0 vs 40.8; HMathA→HMathA acc 50.4 vs 55.3; current part claims GSM8Ks after GSM8K training acc 64.5 vs 68.8. IA2 pipeline: generate ICL response Ŷ using demonstrations from remaining samples; collect A_ICL L×G×d; feed [X∘Ŷ] without demos and train to match activations; then SFT on ground-truth Y.

Paper studies IA2/ICL Activation Alignment: self-distillation matching no-demo activations to own ICL-conditioned activations; priming = IA2 then SFT; IA2+SFT simultaneous. SFT CE over all response tokens. ICL prompt demonstrations + query, no weight updates. asim token-wise cosine over L×R. Earlier results: ICL and SFT activations not aligned, initial/final layers more similar than middle; ICL better calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy. Fig2: SFT-only low asim, IA2→SFT aligns more and performs better. Example numbers: SST2→SST2 acc 65.2 vs 90.4, ECE .22 vs .06; FinS→FinS 67.4 vs 78.7, ECE .31 vs .16; SciQ→SciQ 35.0 vs 40.8; HMathA→HMathA 50.4 vs 55.3; GSM8Ks after GSM8K training 64.5 vs 68.8.

§5 setup: single-token tasks SST2/FinS/PoemS sentiment; STF true/false; AGN/BBCN news; SciQr/QASCr remapped MCQ trained on SciQr. Multi-token: GSM8K/GSM8Ks trained on GSM8K; HMathA; SciQ answer generation. Few-shot N powers of 2, 5 sets per N; IA2 collects A_ICL for each training sample using remaining N−1 samples as demos in random order. Eval separate 500 examples/task. Multi-token uses CoT-style reasoning + answer; parsing: GSM numerical after #### or common patterns; HMathA boxed; SciQ support #### answer exact string. Models: Qwen3-4B-Base every task; Llama-3.2-1B single-token except SciQr uses 3B; multi-token secondary Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. LoRA rank 8 on WQ, WK, WO in SA. Multi-token N up to 16 for Llama, 8 for Qwen; generation cap G=200 for IA2 activations, SFT G=ground-truth token count. Up to 50 epochs, LRs 1e-4/3e-4/1e-3, select best. Single-token acc/ECE from first generated token probs; base ICL averaged over 5 demo sets.

Aggregation replaces Y by response Z and A:Z→aggregation space A; aggregated surrogate risk (3) Rφ,A=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(Xi,Yi)_{i=1}^m); order additional inputs by distance to X, set X_(0)=X; A_{m,K}=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)); Appendix C studies one-sample aggregation.

Consistency definitions: (i) Fisher: Rφ(fn)→Rφ* implies R(fn)→R* for every P. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing ψ with ψ(R(f)-R*)≤Rφ(f)-Rφ*, ψ(ε)>0. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

final_notes:
§4.1 binary: Y={±1}, 0-1, margin surrogate φ(sy); Fisher+uniform iff φ'(0)<0. Prop4: for any ε/nonzero θ*, exists optimally predictable P along θ* s.t. every unaggregated surrogate minimizer has higher task risk than θ* and |cos angle|≤ε. Aggregated binary majority: ε_m-argmin with m→∞ gives R→R(θ*) and cos→1.
§4.2 multiclass: zero-sum linear cone, argmax decoder, limiting loss condition (13). Logistic/pairwise satisfy Fisher consistency+(13). Theorem2: If cone F optimally predicts P, P(Δ(X)>0)=1, ε_m→0, then aggregated majority surrogate risk has R(f_m)→R*.
§4.3 finite-dimensional multiclass: Θ d×(k−1), θ_k=0; link consistency (14): score maximizers iff probability maximizers. Logistic loss (15). For k=2 normal X, Cheng direction consistency under link misspecification. For k≥3, σ^ε definition/prose conflict; claim σ^ε satisfies (14) false on uniform region unless ties. Prop5: for k≥3, Σ=I and invertible D, small ε gives Tε measure ≤ε with unaggregated normalized Θ1≠Θ*. Theorem3: Θ*=U*T*, aggregated Θ_m=U*T_m, ||T_m||→∞, T_m/||T_m||→T*/||T*||.
§5: truncated quadratic/squared hinge φ=max{1−δ,0}², ψ=ε²; aggregated bound δ=1: ψ_m=1/16(ε−sqrt((32/m)log40))_+. Mis-specified logistic experiment k=3,d=2, r=3 α=0.1; Fig2 caption’s error metric conflicts with Theorem3 normalization.
§6: Discussion says many guarantees require m→∞; finite results include ranking Prop2 m≥k and §3.2.3 α=1 O(log k). It notes κ(X)=1 in binary but can be large multiclass, and optimal predictability (12) remains required for §4.3.

Summary claims to track: Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors, for surrogate losses over all measurable predictors and restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Ranking claim: for k≥3 items, no convex surrogate using individual comparisons is Fisher consistent, but an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m≥k. More general claim: identifying surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows. Under noise conditions, aggregation gives approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails, including under link mis-specification. Two numerical illustrations support conclusions. Many guarantees require m→∞. Glossary follows.

Intro/main framing: asks whether label aggregation is necessary and how it improves consistency. Claims aggregation improves consistency of surrogate estimation and can give consistent classifiers in finite-dimensional/restricted problems where standard methods fail. Examples: ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators; estimators using only (X,Y) pairs necessarily fail while aggregation methods are consistent. Section 2 definitions: task risk (1) R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], generalized conditional-distribution risk (2) R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]. Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ℓ(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R=P(Yf(X)≤0). Multiclass conditional loss example ℓ(ŷ,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y} equals 0–1 error. Surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R, Rφ=Eφ(f(X),Y). Consistency settings: Fisher/all Borel measurable functions; restricted/parametric possibly misspecified. Aggregation replaces Y by response Z and A:Z→aggregation space A; aggregated surrogate risk (3) Rφ,A=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. errors.claim: “It is evident that \(\rho_m\) satisfies (14).”
errors.evidence: The part defines majority vote “breaking ties arbitrarily,” while (14) requires \(t_y=\max_i t_i\) iff \(\sigma_y(t)=\max_i\sigma_i(t)\).
errors.explanation: With tied initial scores/probabilities, arbitrary tie-breaking in majority vote can make one tied class have larger majority-vote probability than another. Then a class with maximal score need not have maximal \(\rho_m\)-probability, violating (14).

errors.claim: “This defines a conditional distribution … that samples \(Y\sim\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)\) if \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\), and uniformly otherwise.”
errors.evidence: Immediately before, the definition is \(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\sigma^{\textup{lr}}(t)1\{t\notin\mathcal T_\epsilon\}+\frac1k\mathbf1\cdot1\{t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\}\).
errors.explanation: The formula says the link is logistic outside \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) and uniform inside \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\), but the prose reverses this.

errors.claim: “Clearly \(\sigma^\epsilon\) satisfies (14).”
errors.evidence: The definition sets \(\sigma^\epsilon(t)=\frac1k\mathbf1\) on \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\), while (14) requires maximal scores exactly match maximal probabilities.
errors.explanation: On points \(t\in\mathcal T_\epsilon\) with a unique largest score, the uniform distribution makes every class have maximal probability, so classes with non-maximal scores also have maximal probability. This violates the “if and only if” condition in (14).

errors.claim: “Beyond binary classification, the condition number is smaller than in binary classification even when the Mammen–Tsybakov noise level (Nα) is low, meaning α≈1.”
errors.location: this part, ‘Fundamental limits of the noise condition number’
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says binary classification has “κ(X)=1 trivially,” and its heading says “The condition number can remain large beyond binary classification.” Earlier notes also record: “binary κ=1 if P(Δ>0)=1.”
errors.explanation: If binary κ is trivially 1, saying the multiclass condition number is ‘smaller than in binary classification’ implies κ<1, which conflicts with the discussion that κ can remain large beyond binary classification. The intended comparison appears to be larger, not smaller.

grade.reason: The reviewer’s last reported error identifies the same false claim about the multiclass condition number being smaller than the binary one and notes the direct contradiction with the binary value being 1, matching the planted-error explanation.

errors.claim: “Its minimizers frequently coincide with the original problem (2)”
errors.location: this part, Section 2 after definition of equation (2)
errors.evidence: Immediately before, the text says equation (2) is “a more sophisticated version of (1)” and defines equation (1) as the original task risk depending on labels Y.
errors.explanation: The sentence refers to the ‘original problem’ as (2), but (2) is the newly introduced conditional-distribution formulation. The internally consistent reference would be to original problem (1).

errors.claim: “Define the pointwise and uniform calibration functions: … \(\overline\psi_A(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)\).”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Calibration functions \(\psi(\epsilon,x)=\inf\{\delta_\phi(s,x):\delta_\ell(s,x)\ge\epsilon\}\), \(\overline\psi=\inf_x \psi\).”
errors.explanation: The uniform calibration function should take an infimum over inputs \(x\), not over scores \(s\), because the pointwise function has already minimized over \(s\) and still depends on \(x\). The displayed definition conflicts with the earlier definition of uniform calibration.

Summary claims to track: Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors, for surrogate losses over all measurable predictors and restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Ranking claim: for k≥3 items, no convex surrogate using individual comparisons is Fisher consistent, but an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m≥k. In restricted classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails, including under link mis-specification. Two numerical illustrations support conclusions. steps.notes_before:
Intro/main framing: asks whether label aggregation is necessary and how it improves consistency. Claims aggregation improves consistency of surrogate estimation and can give consistent classifiers in finite-dimensional/restricted problems where standard methods fail. Examples: ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators; estimators using only (X,Y) pairs necessarily fail while aggregation methods are consistent. Claims/evidence summary: ranking impossibility/possibility via Props 1–2 for k≥3 and m≥k; Theorem 1 approximately linear comparison with slope Cφ,1/16 above risk threshold; restricted-class consistency via Corollary 4.1 and Theorem 2 as m→∞.

Section 2 definitions: task risk (1) R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], generalized conditional-distribution risk (2) R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]. Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ℓ(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R=P(Yf(X)≤0). Multiclass conditional loss example ℓ(ŷ,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y} equals 0–1 error. Surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R, Rφ=Eφ(f(X),Y). Consistency settings: Fisher/all Borel measurable functions; restricted/parametric possibly misspecified. Aggregation replaces Y by response Z and A:Z→aggregation space A; aggregated surrogate risk (3) Rφ,A=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Repeated labels: Z=(Y1,…,Ym), conditionally iid; A_m empirical loss minimizer argmin_y Σ_l ℓ(y,Y_l), majority vote for 0–1 loss. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(Xi,Yi)_{i=1}^m); order additional inputs by distance to X, set X_(0)=X; A_{m,K}=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)); Appendix C studies one-sample aggregation.

Earlier technical notes: ranking setup/consistency; identifying surrogate constants; structured prediction embedding/generalized hinge; restricted-class logistic/softmax; numerics as previously noted.

Section 3: standard all-Borel setting. Conditional risks R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), Rφ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]; pointwise excess δℓ,δφ; minimal risks R*,Rφ*. Consistency definitions: (i) Fisher: Rφ(fn)→Rφ* implies R(fn)→R* for every P. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing ψ with ψ(R(f)-R*)≤Rφ(f)-Rφ*, ψ(ε)>0. For binary convex margin surrogates, notions coincide. Calibration functions ψ(ε,x)=inf{δφ(s,x):δℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overlineψ=inf_x ψ. Cor 3.1: φ Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; Fenchel biconjugate of overlineψ gives comparison, and overlineψ(ε)>0 iff biconjugate ψ(ε)>0.

Section 3.1 ranking: label Y=(i,j), i preferred to j. p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x). C_x has C_ii=0, C_ij=p_ij/sum_{l≠j}p_lj, with 0/0=1/(k-1); C_x^T 1=1. Rank by C_x 1 (or powers/Perron variants). Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(e_i-e_j)^T C1≤0 and nonzero}, risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq.4). Scores restricted to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex-in-score φ:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4). Aggregation: with m iid comparisons Z, define counts m_ij, m_j; A(Z)=star if any column count m_j=0, else vector_i Σ_j m_ij/m_j. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

In restricted classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails, including under link mis-specification. Two numerical illustrations support conclusions. Many guarantees require m→∞. Glossary follows.

Summary claims to track: Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors, for surrogate losses over all measurable predictors and restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Ranking claim: for k≥3 items, no convex surrogate using individual comparisons is Fisher consistent, but an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m≥k. More general claim: identifying surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows. Under noise conditions, aggregation gives approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails, including under link mis-specification. Two numerical illustrations support conclusions. Many guarantees require m→∞. Glossary follows.

Summary claims to track: Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors, for surrogate losses over all measurable predictors and restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Ranking claim: for k≥3 items, no convex surrogate using individual comparisons is Fisher consistent, but an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m≥k. More general claim: identifying surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows. Under noise conditions, aggregation gives approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails, including under link mis-specification. Two numerical illustrations support conclusions. Many guarantees require m→∞. Glossary follows.

Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors for surrogate losses, both nonparametric (all measurable/Borel functions) and restricted/parametric classes. Core definitions: task loss ℓ, surrogate φ, decoder d, risks R, Rφ, aggregated surrogate risk Rφ,A; excess risks δ; Fisher consistency = surrogate risk to infimum implies task risk to infimum; uniform comparison/calibration functions ψ, ψ_A, overlineψ_A. Aggregation A maps abstract response Z to aggregation space A; repeated sampling uses m labels, majority/generalized majority vote A_m; KNN aggregation A_{m,K} uses original X plus K nearest among m additional examples.

Counts m_ij,m_j; output star if some m_j=0.

Structured prediction: embedding v:Y→R^d; max-margin/generalized hinge (11); bipartite matching labels size N!; identifiability gap τ(y).

Multiclass logistic with k classes, Θ=[θ1…θ{k−1}], baseline class k score 0, link σ with link consistency (14); majority-vote probabilities ρ_m, p_{Θ,m}. Proposition 5 involves Gaussian inputs, modified logistic link σ^ε on set T_ε of Lebesgue measure ε. Numerical illustrations: truncated quadratic majority-vote comparison ψ_m; corrupted logistic/softmax link with radius r, α=0.1, fixed total labels nm, T=100 trials, 95% error bars.

Summary claims to track: Paper studies whether aggregating noisy labels improves consistency of learned predictors, for surrogate losses over all measurable predictors and restricted model classes. Develops calibration inequalities for aggregated labels; analyzes ranking, classification, structured prediction. Ranking claim: for k≥3 items, no convex surrogate using individual comparisons is Fisher consistent, but an aggregated squared-loss procedure is consistent when m≥k. More general claim: identifying surrogates become asymptotically consistent as number m of aggregated labels grows. Under noise conditions, aggregation gives approximately linear comparison inequalities. In restricted classes, aggregation can restore consistency when ordinary surrogate minimization fails, including under link mis-specification. Two numerical illustrations support conclusions. Many guarantees require m→∞. Glossary follows.

Section 2 definitions: task risk (1) R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], generalized conditional-distribution risk (2) R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]. Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ℓ(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R=P(Yf(X)≤0). Multiclass conditional loss example ℓ(ŷ,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y} equals 0–1 error. Surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R, Rφ=Eφ(f(X),Y). Consistency settings: Fisher/all Borel measurable functions; restricted/parametric possibly misspecified. Aggregation replaces Y by response Z and A:Z→aggregation space A; aggregated surrogate risk (3) Rφ,A=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Repeated labels: Z=(Y1,…,Ym), conditionally iid; A_m empirical loss minimizer argmin_y Σ_l ℓ(y,Y_l), majority vote for 0–1 loss. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(Xi,Yi)_{i=1}^m); order additional inputs by distance to X, set X_(0)=X; A_{m,K}=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)); Appendix C studies one-sample aggregation.

Earlier technical notes: ranking setup/consistency; identifying surrogate constants; structured prediction embedding/generalized hinge; restricted-class logistic/softmax; numerics as previously noted.

Section 3: standard all-Borel setting. Conditional risks R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), Rφ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]; pointwise excess δℓ,δφ; minimal risks R*,Rφ*. Consistency definitions: (i) Fisher: Rφ(fn)→Rφ* implies R(fn)→R* for every P. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing ψ with ψ(R(f)-R*)≤Rφ(f)-Rφ*, ψ(ε)>0. For binary convex margin surrogates, notions coincide. Calibration functions ψ(ε,x)=inf{δφ(s,x):δℓ(s,x)≥ε}, overlineψ=inf_x ψ. Cor 3.1: φ Fisher consistent iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε>0; Fenchel biconjugate of overlineψ gives comparison, and overlineψ(ε)>0 iff biconjugate ψ(ε)>0.

Section 3.1 ranking: label Y=(i,j), i preferred to j. p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x). C_x has C_ii=0, C_ij=p_ij/sum_{l≠j}p_lj, with 0/0=1/(k-1); C_x^T 1=1. Rank by C_x 1 (or powers/Perron variants). Loss ℓ(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(e_i-e_j)^T C1≤0 and nonzero}, risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq.4). Scores restricted to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex-in-score φ:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4). Aggregation: with m iid comparisons Z, define counts m_ij, m_j; A(Z)=star if any column count m_j=0, else vector_i Σ_j m_ij/m_j. Proposition 2: squared-loss regression on A(Z) is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

final_notes:
Paper studies alignment/post-training effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = post-trained with reward/preference/aesthetic models; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval tuple <p,a,c>, 42 verbs. Persistent inconsistency: Sec 3.1 claimed 4 gender categories × 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs, but Sec 3.2/Table 1 only Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt conditions. Sec 5.2 introduced Ethnicity+Gender image benchmark with Table 3 #prompts Ethnicity+Person 294, Ethnicity+Gender 1176 despite Sec 3.2 lacking that condition.

Metrics: TAS=% frames matching final majority label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), range [-1,1]. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; min −0.1429; SDI=1−sum P_e^2. Several RDS tables/claims have impossible values below −1/7, including Table 5 VCM-VC2 Black -0.2381, East Asian -0.2333, Middle Eastern -0.1690.

Table 2 Avg PBSG: ModelScope .4815→Instruct .5295; VideoCrafter .7581→T2V .8306. Table 4 reward PBSG: CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.0 .6039, HPSv2.1 -.0984, PickScore -.1157. Table 5 VCM-VC2 PBSG base .8034, HPSv2.0 .9116, HPSv2.1 .2267, PickScore .3714; SDI base .1433, HPSv2.0 .1257, HPSv2.1 .0976, PickScore .1467. Conflict: female-skewed rewards but male-skewed aligned videos for HPSv2.1/PickScore.

Sec 7 controlled preference datasets RMM/RMW. Table 7 “PBSG” has impossible RMM avg 1.5280 >1; RMW -0.7448. Table 8 video PBSG: VCM .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082, so RMW reduces but does not reverse male skew. Broader Impact repeats these claims and overstates “opposite directions” for video portrayals. Acknowledgment adds only funding/disclaimer, no relevant technical claims.

Paper summary: investigates how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, event-based eval separating actor attributes from verbs/contexts. Measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Claims preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. Also constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set.

Paper investigates how alignment tuning/post-training optimization toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting/evaluation where an event is an actor performing a verb in a context, controlling actor demographic attributes separately from verbs/contexts. Social attributes analyzed are gender and ethnicity; includes ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic group). Frame-level VLM-judge ensemble classifies gender/ethnicity; video-level labels via majority vote. Temporal issues include attribute flickering; TAS and perfect stability reported later (Table 6). Uniform/parity reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim.

Alignment terms: aligned model = preference-guided post-training; unaligned = likelihood-based baseline. Reward/preference models trained from human-labeled image comparisons guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning, RLHF/RL-style alternatives). Aesthetic reward and image reward feedback used in Latent Consistency Distillation from teacher to student for single-step video generation.

Claims from earlier summary: preference datasets and reward models can inherit/amplify biases and make portrayals more temporally stable. Constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract existing gender bias. Counter-biased reward model/controllable preference modeling can steer demographic distributions; dual-use risk (mitigate bias or exclude groups). errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Person-only tests which gender/ethnicity models assign without explicit cues; ethnicity+person tests explicit ethnicity and inferred attributes such as gender.”
errors.explanation: For person-only prompts, observed demographic disparities cannot be attributed to demographic conditioning because no demographic condition is provided. The statement overgeneralizes across both prompt types.

errors.claim: RDS values such as Black RDS = -0.1952, Latino RDS = -0.1952, and T2V-Turbo-V1 Latino RDS = -0.2476
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e = P_e - 1/7, uniform 14.3%.” Since P_e is a proportion, the minimum possible RDS is 0 - 1/7 ≈ -0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several RDS entries in Table 2 are below the mathematically possible minimum under the paper’s own definition of RDS.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e = P_e - 1/7,” where P_e is the proportion of identifiable ethnicity. If a model generated zero recognizable instances of an ethnicity, P_e = 0 and RDS_e = -1/7, so the metric is still computable.
errors.explanation: The caption says zero recognizable instances make RDS uncomputable, but the paper’s own formula defines RDS for zero instances.

errors.claim: “InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1 show PBSG increases of 0.04 and 0.0725, respectively.”
errors.location: this part, Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias paragraph
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the Average PBSG delta for InstructVideo as +0.0480, not +0.04.
errors.explanation: The stated InstructVideo PBSG increase does not match the table value; +0.0480 would normally round to +0.05, not +0.04.

errors.claim: “They verify whether content reflects the prompted attribute” while verifying “gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Sec 3.2 uses only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person prompts; actor always “person” or ethnicity+“person”; no gender prompts.
errors.explanation: Gender was not a prompted attribute in the described prompt sets, so human annotators could not verify whether generated gender reflected a prompted gender attribute.

errors.claim: “Core bias metrics remain statistically stable: PBSG changes from 0.846 to 0.863, p=0.68; SDI changes from 0.745 to 0.761. This non-significant difference confirms that residual evaluator uncertainty does not distort the reported measurements.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 2 reported Overall SDI values: ModelScope 0.0538, InstructVideo 0.0267, VideoCrafter-2 0.1252, T2V-Turbo-V1 0.1119.
errors.explanation: The SDI values claimed here, 0.745 and 0.761, are far from the previously reported SDI measurements for the evaluated models. Unless a different dataset/definition is being used, this conflicts with the paper’s own reported SDI scale/results.

errors.claim: “Figure 3: Image reward datasets gender preference distribution across 42 verbs” and “Figure 4: Image reward datasets ethnicity preference across 42 verbs.”
errors.evidence: The same section says: “After processing, HPDv2 has 28,783 ... tuples covering 29 verbs. Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples covering 19 verbs.”
errors.explanation: The part says the retained preference datasets cover only 29 and 19 verbs, but then describes their gender/ethnicity preference distributions as across 42 verbs. Unless empty/non-retained verbs are being included, this overstates the verb coverage.

errors.claim: “We use ... the event templates from Section 3.2. The benchmark varies gender, ethnicity, and verb... Ethnicity+Gender: both ethnicity and gender are explicit.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Sec 3.2 uses only Person-only (42) and Ethnicity+Person (294); actor always ‘person’ or ethnicity+‘person,’ no gender prompts.”
errors.explanation: This part says the benchmark uses Section 3.2 event templates while including an Ethnicity+Gender setting, but Section 3.2’s prompt settings did not include gender-explicit templates.

errors.claim: “PickScore favors East Asian representation, RDS = 0.0352.”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports PickScore East Asian RDS = 0.0316, not 0.0352. The largest PickScore RDS in the table is East Asian at 0.0316, with Black RDS = 0.0279, Southeast Asian = 0.0115, White = 0.0069, and others negative.
errors.explanation: The text’s qualitative statement that PickScore favors East Asian representation is supported by the table, but the reported numeric RDS value conflicts with Table 4.

errors.claim: The prose reports PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0352.
errors.evidence: Table 4: “PickScore, East Asian RDS 0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The prose value for PickScore’s East Asian RDS conflicts with the Table 4 value reported in the same part.

errors.claim: “Under the ethnicity-only condition, we use RDSe and SDI to assess balance.”
errors.evidence: The table caption says missing RDS values occur “under the person-only condition (i.e., when ethnicity is not explicitly specified).” Earlier notes also record that Sec. 3.2 uses “Person-only and Ethnicity+Person prompts,” not an ethnicity-only condition.
errors.explanation: The paper’s evaluation condition for ethnic representation is person-only/no ethnicity specified, not ethnicity-only. This sentence contradicts both the table explanation in this part and the earlier recorded setup.

errors.claim: “HPSv2.1 improves balance for White and Black groups but significantly reduces Latino representation, RDS = –0.4352.”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +HPSv2.1 row has Latino RDS marked “—”; the value –0.4352 appears in the Δ row under “Latino PBSG,” not Latino RDS.
errors.explanation: The text misidentifies a PBSG change as a Latino RDS value. Table 5 provides no Latino RDS for HPSv2.1.

errors.claim: “the prose calls –0.4352 Latino RDS” / earlier prose reportedly says “HPSv2.1 Latino RDS = -0.4352.”
errors.evidence: This part states: “Table 5, + HPSv2.1 row: White RDS 0.4286; Black RDS —; Latino RDS —. Its Δ row gives Latino PBSG -0.4352; the prose calls –0.4352 Latino RDS.” Earlier notes also record: “says HPSv2.1 Latino RDS=-.4352 but table has Latino RDS missing and -.4352 is Latino PBSG delta.”
errors.explanation: The value -0.4352 is identified as the Latino PBSG delta, while Latino RDS is missing. Calling it Latino RDS contradicts Table 5.

errors.claim: “RMW substantially lowers it, indicating a strong shift toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +RMW PBSG values that are still positive for every group: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. The same section treats positive PBSG as male preference: “The base generator, such as VCM-VC2, already has pronounced male bias” with VCM-VC2 Average 0.8034, and “RMM raises PBSG ... and reinforces male preference.”
errors.explanation: The table supports that RMW reduces male bias, but not that the aligned generator shifts to woman preference; all reported PBSG values remain positive, i.e. still on the male-preference side by the section’s own interpretation.

errors.claim: “Beyond binary control, the results suggest a continuous alignment axis: mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data yield tunable trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence.”
errors.evidence: Later in the same part: “Mixtures of preference data are proposed as a further control mechanism. Tables 7–8 establish the two directional endpoints; this section presents mixture-based optimization as a promising direction, not a reported mixture experiment.”
errors.explanation: The opening states that mixtures yield tunable trade-offs as if this is a result, but the later claims-and-evidence section says mixtures were not experimentally reported and are only proposed as a future/promising control mechanism.

errors.claim: “Curated preference data can steer social portrayals in opposite directions.”
errors.location: this part, Claims and evidence bullet 2
errors.evidence: This part cites Table 8: “Average video PBSG: + RMM 0.9584; + RMW 0.3082.” Earlier notes: “Error: text says RMW shifts video generation toward woman preference, but Table 8 all PBSG values remain positive, so only reduced male bias.”
errors.explanation: The cited video-generation results do not show opposite directions: both PBSG values are positive, indicating male preference remains for both RMM and RMW. RMW mitigates/reduces male bias relative to baseline/RMM, but does not steer video portrayals in the opposite direction.

final_notes:
Paper studies alignment/post-training effects on social representation in video diffusion. VideoBiasEval: 42 verbs; ethnicities White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. Prompt inconsistency: Sec 3.1 mentions gender categories man/woman/person/non-binary, but Sec 3.2 uses Person-only and Ethnicity+Person only.

VLM judges: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; 16 frames/video. Gender labels {man,woman}; ethnicity labels 7 groups. Metrics: TAS, PBSG, RDS, SDI. RDS formula/min issue: formula P_e-1/7 but Table 2 has lower values; zero ethnicity makes RDS missing.

Sec 4 Table 2: Avg PBSG ModelScope .4815→InstructVideo .5295; VideoCrafter .7581→T2V .8306. Human eval SDI .745→.761, far from Table 2.

Sec 5.1: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs, but figures described across 42 verbs. FLUX benchmark: Ethnicity+Person 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 prompts; 100 images/prompt. Table 4 PickScore East Asian RDS .0316; prose wrongly says .0352. Conclusion says qualifying verbs: HPDv2 18/26 favor men; Pick-a-Pic 11/18 favor women; avg PBSG HPSv2.0 .6039, PickScore -.1157.

Sec 6: Table 5 VCM-VC2 PBSG .8034 SDI .1433; +HPSv2.0 .9116/.1257; +HPSv2.1 .2267/.0976; +PickScore .3714/.1467. Error: prose says ethnicity-only though table says person-only; says HPSv2.1 Latino RDS=-.4352 but Latino RDS missing and -.4352 is Latino PBSG delta.

Sec 7: Table 7 reward PBSG CLIP -0.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW -0.7448. Table 8 video PBSG VCM .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. Error repeated in broader impact: RMW reduces male bias but does not shift video PBSG opposite/female because still positive. Mixture trade-offs proposed, not experimentally shown.

Limitations: five listed limitations. Broader Impact: argues alignment stabilizes bias; dual-use risks; no numerical deployment evidence for normalization/exclusion/propaganda risks. Acknowledgment lists funding/support and disclaimer; no conflicts noted.

Summary claims: Paper studies how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based evaluation framework that separates actor attributes from verbs and contexts. Authors examine human preference datasets, image reward models trained on those datasets, and video models aligned with those rewards. Reported findings: preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. They also construct man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Metrics include ethnicity bias, ethnicity-aware gender bias (gender imbalance within ethnic groups), bias shift after alignment, and temporal stability/coherence (attribute flickering; TAS/perfect stability later). Evaluation is multi-granular: frame-level VLM classification of gender/ethnicity, aggregated to video-level labels by majority voting; VLMs-as-judges ensemble, with human verification using Pearson correlation and kappa metrics. Uniform/parity reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim. Models: unaligned baseline trained with likelihood-based objective; aligned model undergoes preference-guided post-training optimization. Reward/preference models/functions are trained from human-labeled image comparison pairs (preferred/dispreferred image matching caption) and guide optimization, including reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style alternatives. They examine human preference datasets, image reward models, and video models aligned with those rewards. They construct man-preferred and woman-preferred/counter-biased reward datasets; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract an existing gender bias. Glossary mentions controllable preference modeling/data composition, normalized sensitivity = action’s PBSG change divided by reward model baseline PBSG, softmax to normalize reward scores across ethnicities, standardized scores, Latent Consistency Distillation with image-reward feedback, teacher/student model, single-step video generation. errors.claim: “We combine four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs.” / “the four gender-prompt categories are man, woman, the neutral term person, and non-binary person.”
errors.evidence: Section 3.2 says “We use two conditions: 1. Person-only ... 42 prompts total. 2. Ethnicity+Person ... 294 prompts.” Table 1 likewise lists only “Person Only” and “Ethnicity + Person,” with no man, woman, or non-binary person prompt conditions.
errors.explanation: The part claims the prompt/evaluation space combines four gender-prompt categories, but the actual prompting protocol and prompt counts only instantiate “person” plus ethnicity descriptors. The other three gender categories are defined but not used in the stated prompt conditions.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation. All demographic analysis occurs afterward.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Section 3.2/Table 1 only define two video prompt conditions: Person Only = 42 prompts, Ethnicity+Person = 294 prompts”; this part also later says labels “support evaluation against prompted attributes” and discusses “ethnicity-conditioned verbs.”
errors.explanation: Ethnicity is explicitly included in the Ethnicity+Person prompts, so demographic attributes are introduced/conditioned during at least part of generation, not only analyzed afterward.

errors.claim: “Fixed prompts make it possible to attribute observed disparities to demographic conditioning rather than uncontrolled contextual drift.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Table 1 has “Person Only = 42 prompts, Ethnicity+Person = 294 prompts”; the current part says demographic attributes are “not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.explanation: The paper cannot both say disparities are attributable to demographic conditioning in fixed prompts and say demographic attributes are not introduced or constrained during generation.

errors.claim: “A value of 0.5 means men occur twice as often as women: N_man = 3N_woman.”
errors.evidence: The same sentence states “twice as often” and “N_man = 3N_woman”; under the given formula PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_total), PBSG=0.5 implies N_man=3N_woman.
errors.explanation: The equation and stated ratio imply men occur three times as often as women, not twice as often.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications…”
errors.evidence: The surrounding subsection is titled “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias” and defines PBSG; it says “Computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition tests whether gender disparities vary across ethnicities.” Earlier notes also record generated average PBSG results.
errors.explanation: The paper says it excludes gender bias from the analysis while simultaneously defining and reporting gender-bias analysis via PBSG.

errors.claim: “Computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition tests whether gender disparities vary across ethnicities.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Section 3.2/Table 1 only define two video prompt conditions: Person Only = 42 prompts, Ethnicity+Person = 294 prompts; no man/woman/non-binary prompt conditions.”
errors.explanation: The paper refers to an ethnicity+gender condition, but the recorded prompt conditions include ethnicity+person, not ethnicity+gender.

errors.claim: Several RDS values in Table 2 are below -0.1429, e.g. Black RDS = -0.1952, Latino RDS = -0.1952, T2V-Turbo-V1 Latino RDS = -0.2476.

Paper summary: investigates how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, event-based eval separating actor attributes from verbs/contexts. Examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Claims preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. Also constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set.

Paper investigates how alignment tuning/post-training optimization toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting/evaluation where an event is an actor performing a verb in a context, controlling actor demographic attributes separately from verbs/contexts. Social attributes analyzed are gender and ethnicity; includes ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic group). Frame-level VLM-judge ensemble classifies gender/ethnicity; video-level labels via majority vote. Temporal issues include attribute flickering; TAS and perfect stability reported later (Table 6). Reward/preference models trained from human-labeled image comparisons guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning, RLHF/RL-style alternatives). Normalized sensitivity = action’s PBSG change divided by reward model baseline PBSG. Softmax normalizes reward scores across ethnicities; standardized score uses mean/std. The other three gender categories are defined but not used in the stated prompt conditions.

errors.claim: “demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation. All demographic analysis occurs afterward.”

errors.explanation: The paper previously described an Ethnicity+Person prompt condition, meaning ethnicity is explicitly introduced during generation. The current statement that demographic attributes are not introduced or constrained during generation contradicts that setup.

errors.explanation: The footnote says gender bias is excluded from this analysis, but the subsection and reported results explicitly analyze gender bias using PBSG.

errors.claim: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/7” (definition from earlier notes) and Table 2 reports RDS values such as Black RDS = -0.1952, Middle Eastern RDS = -0.1976, and T2V-Turbo-V1 Latino RDS = -0.2476.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e=P_e−1/7.” Since P_e is a proportion, its minimum is 0, so RDS_e cannot be less than −1/7 ≈ −0.1429. Table 2 contains multiple RDS values below −0.1429.

final_notes:
Paper studies post-training/alignment effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = reward/preference/aesthetic post-trained; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval: 42 verbs; inconsistency: Sec 3.1 claimed 4 genders × 7 ethnicities × 42, but actual conditions are Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt condition. final_notes:
Paper studies alignment/post-training effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = reward/preference/aesthetic post-training; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval uses <p,a,c>, 42 verbs. Earlier inconsistency: Sec 3.1 claimed 4 gender categories × 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs, but Sec 3.2/Table 1 only Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt conditions; also says demographics not constrained despite ethnicity prompts.

Metrics: TAS=% frames matching final majority. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), bounded [-1,1]. RDS_e=P_e−1/7, min −.1429; SDI=1−sum P_e^2. Errors: Tables 2/5 include impossible RDS below −1/7.

Reward data: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs, Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19. Pick-a-Pic inconsistency: Sec 5.1 prose said 51.11%, but 11/18 and conclusion say 61.11% woman-preferred. Generated avg PBSG baseline .8034; +HPSv2 .9116; +HPSv2.1 .2267; +PickScore .3714. Controlled PBSG baseline .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082.

Human eval: 400 videos; Pearson .89/.73; κ .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82. FLUX Table 4 Avg PBSG CLIP −.0726, HPSv2.0 .6039, HPSv2.1 −.0984, PickScore −.1157; SDI ~.847–.849. Error: prose says PickScore East Asian RDS .0352, table .0316.

Sec 6/Table 5 errors: HPSv2.1 Black balance claim despite missing Black RDS; Latino RDS=−.4352 claim but table has Latino RDS “—” and −.4352 is Δ Latino PBSG.

Sec 7/Broader Impact: RMM/RMW trained on 2.94M gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2. Table 7 reward “PBSG” includes impossible RMM avg 1.5280 (>1); Broader Impact repeats it. RMW lowers male bias but video PBSG remains positive (.3082), not woman-preferred. Mixture tuning claimed as result but only proposed. Broader Impact says alignment stabilizes bias, dual-use risks, audit/curation responsibility; no numerical deployment evidence for normalization/exclusion/propaganda risks.

Acknowledgment lists AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; views not official endorsements.

Paper summary: investigates how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, event-based eval separating actor attributes from verbs/contexts. Measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Claims preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. Also constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set.

Paper investigates how alignment tuning/post-training optimization toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting/evaluation where an event is an actor performing a verb in a context, controlling actor demographic attributes separately from verbs/contexts. Social attributes analyzed are gender and ethnicity; includes ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic group). Frame-level VLM-judge ensemble classifies gender/ethnicity; video-level labels via majority vote. Temporal issues include attribute flickering; TAS and perfect stability reported later (Table 6). Uniform/parity reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim.

Alignment terms: aligned model = preference-guided post-training; unaligned = likelihood-based baseline. Reward/preference models trained from human-labeled image comparisons guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning, RLHF/RL-style alternatives). Aesthetic reward and image reward feedback used in Latent Consistency Distillation from teacher to student for single-step video generation.

Claims from earlier summary: preference datasets and reward models can inherit/amplify biases and make portrayals more temporally stable. Constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract existing gender bias. Counter-biased reward model/controllable preference modeling can steer demographic distributions; dual-use risk (mitigate bias or exclude groups). Normalized sensitivity = action’s PBSG change divided by reward model baseline PBSG. Softmax normalizes reward scores across ethnicities; standardized score uses mean/std. Human verification reports Pearson correlation, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa; sensitivity analyses include high-agreement subsets/action-level responses. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set; future intersectional attributes/multi-turn video instruction alignment.

final_notes:
Paper studies alignment/post-training effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = reward/preference/aesthetic post-trained; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval has 42 verbs/actions. Earlier inconsistency: Sec 3.1 claimed 4 gender categories × 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs, but Sec 3.2/Table 1 only Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt conditions; ethnicity+gender condition not defined; footnote says exclude gender bias despite PBSG analysis.

Metrics: PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), + male, − female; range [-1,1]. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; SDI=1−sum P_e^2. RDS below −1/7 impossible; Tables 2 and 5 contain impossible RDS values.

Sec 4/Table 2: ModelScope PBSG .4815; InstructVideo .5295, Δ +.0480, but prose said +.1480. Human eval SDI .745→.761 conflicts with Table 2 SDI scale.

Sec 5.1: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs, but captions say 42 verbs. HPDv2 gender pairs: 26 valid, 18 male-preferred (69.23%); Pick-a-Pic: 18 valid, 11 female-preferred (61.11%).

Sec 5.2/Table 4: CLIP PBSG -0.0726 SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 .6039; HPSv2.1 -.0984; PickScore -.1157. PickScore East Asian RDS prose .0352 vs table .0316.

Sec 6/Table 5 VCM-VC2: base PBSG .8034 SDI .1433; +HPS2.0 .9116; +HPS2.1 .2267; +PickScore .3714.

Sec 7: RMM/RMW from alleged Ethnicity+Gender set; RMM Table 7 PBSG values >1 impossible, avg 1.5280; Broad Impact repeats this impossible value. Table 8: VCM .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper summary: investigates how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, event-based eval separating actor attributes from verbs/contexts. Measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Claims preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. Also constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set.

Paper investigates how alignment tuning/post-training optimization toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting/evaluation where an event is an actor performing a verb in a context, controlling actor demographic attributes separately from verbs/contexts. Social attributes analyzed are gender and ethnicity; includes ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic group). Frame-level VLM-judge ensemble classifies gender/ethnicity; video-level labels via majority vote. Temporal issues include attribute flickering; TAS and perfect stability reported later (Table 6). Uniform/parity reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim.

Alignment terms: aligned model = preference-guided post-training; unaligned = likelihood-based baseline. Reward/preference models trained from human-labeled image comparisons guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning, RLHF/RL-style alternatives). Aesthetic reward and image reward feedback used in Latent Consistency Distillation from teacher to student for single-step video generation.

Claims from earlier summary: preference datasets and reward models can inherit/amplify biases and make portrayals more temporally stable. Constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract existing gender bias. Counter-biased reward model/controllable preference modeling can steer demographic distributions; dual-use risk (mitigate bias or exclude groups). Normalized sensitivity = action’s PBSG change divided by reward model baseline PBSG. Softmax normalizes reward scores across ethnicities; standardized score uses mean/std. Human verification reports Pearson correlation, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa; sensitivity analyses include high-agreement subsets/action-level responses. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set; future intersectional attributes/multi-turn video instruction alignment.

Paper investigates how alignment/post-training toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. errors.claim: “The prose reports the first increase as 0.04.”
errors.evidence: The same bullet gives Table 2 Δ rows for Average PBSG as “+0.0480 and +0.0725.” Earlier notes also record: “text says Instruct PBSG increase .04 vs table .0480.”

errors.claim: “Figure 3: Image reward datasets gender preference distribution across 42 verbs.” / “Figure 4: Image reward datasets ethnicity preference across 42 verbs.”
errors.evidence: The same section says: “After processing, HPDv2 has 28,783 ... tuples covering 29 verbs. Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples covering 19 verbs.” It also says for gender: “In HPDv2, 26 out of 42 verbs have valid man–woman pairs” and “In Pick-a-Pic, 18 out of 42 qualify.”

errors.claim: “We use FLUX ... and the event templates from Section 3.2” to construct two settings including “Ethnicity+Gender,” with Table 3 listing 1176 prompts.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Sec 3.2/Table 1 only Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt conditions,” and “references to ethnicity+gender condition not defined.”

errors.claim: “PickScore favors East Asian representation, RDS = 0.0352.”

errors.claim: The prose reports PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0352.

errors.claim: RDS values such as Black RDS = -0.2381, East Asian RDS = -0.2333, Middle Eastern RDS = -0.1690 for VCM-VC2; Middle Eastern RDS = -0.3667 for +HPSv2.0; Middle Eastern RDS = -0.4286 for +HPSv2.1; etc.

errors.claim: “RMW substantially lowers it, indicating a strong shift toward woman preference.”

errors.claim: “Table 7, Average: CLIP -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448.”

errors.claim: “Beyond binary control, the results suggest a continuous alignment axis: mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data yield tunable trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence.”

errors.claim: “Our analyses show that reward-based alignment inherits, and frequently amplifies, biases in human preference data.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Sec 6 reward-profile causal claim conflicts with HPSv2.1/PickScore rewards female-skewed while aligned videos male-skewed.” Specifically, Table 4 PickScore Average PBSG = -0.1157, but Table 5 PickScore-aligned VCM-VC2 Average PBSG = 0.3714; HPSv2.1 reward PBSG = -0.0984, but HPSv2.1-aligned VCM-VC2 PBSG = 0.2267.
errors.explanation: The paper’s own reported reward-model biases for PickScore and HPSv2.1 are female-skewed, while the corresponding aligned video models are male-skewed. errors.claim: “Table 7, Average reward PBSG: RMM 1.5280”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition: “PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), bounded [-1,1].”
errors.explanation: A PBSG value of 1.5280 is impossible under the paper’s own PBSG definition, so this reported Table 7 value contradicts the metric bounds.

errors.claim: “Curated preference data can steer social portrayals in opposite directions. … Table 8, Average video PBSG: + RMM 0.9584; + RMW 0.3082.”

Paper studies alignment/post-training effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = post-trained with reward/preference/aesthetic models; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval tuple <p,a,c>, 42 verbs/actions. Persistent inconsistency: Sec 3.1 claimed 4 gender categories × 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs, but Sec 3.2/Table 1 only Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt conditions. Sec 5.2/Table 3 introduced Ethnicity+Gender image benchmark #prompts Ethnicity+Person 294, Ethnicity+Gender 1176 despite Sec 3.2 lacking it.

Metrics: TAS=% frames matching final majority label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), bounded [-1,1]. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; min −0.1429; SDI=1−sum P_e^2. Several RDS values impossible below −1/7, incl. Table 5 VCM-VC2 Black -0.2381, East Asian -0.2333, Middle Eastern -0.1690.

Table 2 avg PBSG: ModelScope .4815→Instruct .5295; VideoCrafter .7581→T2V .8306. Reward/image benchmark: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs; Fig captions wrongly said 42 verbs. Table 4 reward PBSG: CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.0 .6039, HPSv2.1 -.0984, PickScore -.1157.

Sec 6/Table 5 VCM-VC2 PBSG: base .8034, HPSv2.0 .9116, HPSv2.1 .2267, PickScore .3714. Claim alignment inherits reward bias conflicts with HPSv2.1/PickScore rewards female-skewed while aligned videos male-skewed.

Sec 7: RMM/RMW pair count inconsistent: 29.4M vs 2.94M. Table 7 calls values PBSG but RMM average 1.5280 >1 impossible. Table 8: RMW lowers PBSG .8034→.3082 but remains positive for all groups, so not woman-preference/opposite direction. Part 19 overstated mixtures as yielding trade-offs, then says mixtures only proposed, not tested. Broader Impact repeats impossible RMM PBSG and overclaims opposite video steering. Acknowledgment only funding/disclaimer; no new technical claims.

Paper summary: investigates how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, event-based eval separating actor attributes from verbs/contexts. Measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Claims preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. Also constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set.

Paper investigates how alignment tuning/post-training optimization toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting/evaluation where an event is an actor performing a verb in a context, controlling actor demographic attributes separately from verbs/contexts. Social attributes analyzed are gender and ethnicity; includes ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic group). Frame-level VLM-judge ensemble classifies gender/ethnicity; video-level labels via majority vote. Temporal issues include attribute flickering; TAS and perfect stability reported later (Table 6). Uniform/parity reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim.

Reward/preference models trained from human-labeled image comparisons guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning, RLHF/RL-style alternatives). final_notes:
Paper studies alignment/post-training effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = reward/preference/aesthetic post-trained; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval: fixed 42 socially associated actions; limitations acknowledge predefined identity categories, VLM evaluator biases, single-step latent consistency distillation w/ limited reward models, synthetic gender-preference interventions, limited action coverage. Inconsistency: Sec 3.1 said 4 genders × 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs, but Sec 3.2/Table 1 only Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt condition. Sec 5.2 image benchmark adds Ethnicity+Gender 1176.

Metrics: video PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male skew; image PBSG standardized reward difference, can exceed 1. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; min −.1429; SDI=1−sum P_e^2.

Known errors: impossible RDS below −1/7; Fig 3/4 wrongly say 42 verbs for image prefs; Table 4 prose wrongly says CLIP lowest SDI though CLIP .8495 highest; Table 2 prose misstates strongest imbalance/PBSG increase.

Table 2 video avg PBSG: ModelScope .4815→Instruct .5295; VideoCrafter .7581→T2V .8306. Table 4 image avg PBSG: CLIP −.0726, HPSv2.0 .6039, HPSv2.1 −.0984, PickScore −.1157. Sec 6 VCM-VC2 avg PBSG base .8034; +HPS2.0 .9116; +HPS2.1 .2267; +Pick .3714. SDI base .1433; HPS2.0 .1257; HPS2.1 .0976; Pick .1467. Table 6 gender stability: mean TAS .9763→.9967 and perfect stability .8850→.9830 for HPS2.0.

Sec 7: Table7 CLIP avg reward PBSG −.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW −.7448. Table8 video PBSG VCM .8034, +RMM .9584, +RMW .3082; RMW reduces but remains positive male skew overall. Error: says mixtures yield tunable trade-offs, but later says mixtures only proposed, not tested. Broader Impact repeats dual-use claims and states propaganda/exclusion risks without numerical deployment evidence. Acknowledgment: funding/support only; no contradictions noted.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper summary: investigates how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, event-based eval separating actor attributes from verbs/contexts. Measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Claims preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. Also constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set.

Paper investigates how alignment tuning/post-training optimization toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting/evaluation where an event is an actor performing a verb in a context, controlling actor demographic attributes separately from verbs/contexts. Social attributes analyzed are gender and ethnicity; includes ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic group). Frame-level VLM-judge ensemble classifies gender/ethnicity; video-level labels via majority vote. Temporal issues include attribute flickering; TAS and perfect stability reported later (Table 6). Uniform/parity reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim.

Alignment terms: aligned model = preference-guided post-training; unaligned = likelihood-based baseline. Reward/preference models trained from human-labeled image comparisons guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning, RLHF/RL-style alternatives). Aesthetic reward and image reward feedback used in Latent Consistency Distillation from teacher to student for single-step video generation.

Claims from earlier summary: preference datasets and reward models can inherit/amplify biases and make portrayals more temporally stable. Constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract existing gender bias. Counter-biased reward model/controllable preference modeling can steer demographic distributions; dual-use risk (mitigate bias or exclude groups). Normalized sensitivity = action’s PBSG change divided by reward model baseline PBSG. Softmax normalizes reward scores across ethnicities; standardized score uses mean/std. Human verification reports Pearson correlation, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa; sensitivity analyses include high-agreement subsets/action-level responses. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set; future intersectional attributes/multi-turn video instruction alignment.

Paper investigates how alignment/post-training toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. VideoBiasEval: event tuple <p,a,c> = actor/person p, verb/action a, context c; prompt slots include [actor]/[verb]/[context] and [ethnicity]/[gender]/[action]. Social attributes: gender and ethnicity, including ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. VLM judges output binary gender labels G={man,woman}; gender prompt categories include Man, Woman, Person, Non-binary person. Ethnicity set E has 7 labels: White, Black, Indian (tables may label column “India”), East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino.

Key metrics/symbols: PBSG/PBS_G = (N_man−N_woman or video-count difference)/total, range [-1,1]; in reward-model evaluation it can mean standardized reward-score difference. N_total = men+women for PBSG or identifiable-ethnicity outputs for ethnicity metrics. P_e=N_e/N_total. RDS_e/RDSe/RDS = P_e−1/|E|; RDSWhite for White. SDI=1−sum_e P_e^2. TAS = percent frames matching final majority-voted video attribute label. Δ metrics are changes vs unaligned/baseline. “—” in ethnicity metrics means no recognizable instances under person-only prompting. errors.claim: “demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation. All demographic analysis occurs afterward.”

errors.explanation: The paper previously described an Ethnicity+Person prompt condition, meaning ethnicity is explicitly introduced during generation. The current statement that demographic attributes are not introduced or constrained during generation contradicts that setup.

errors.claim: “Footnote 1. We exclude gender bias from this analysis...”

errors.explanation: The footnote says gender bias is excluded from this analysis, but the subsection and reported results explicitly analyze gender bias using PBSG.

errors.claim: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/7” (definition from earlier parts); Table 2 reports RDS values such as Black RDS = -0.1952 and Latino RDS = -0.2476.

final_notes:
Paper studies post-training/alignment effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = reward/preference/aesthetic post-trained; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval: 42 actions. Earlier inconsistency: Sec 3.1 claimed 4 gender categories × 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs, but Table 1 only Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt conditions. RDS_e=P_e−1/7, min −0.1429; many RDS values violate this. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), bounded [-1,1].

Sec 5 datasets: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs, despite figures saying 42 verbs. Reward Table 4: CLIP PBSG -0.0726 SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 .6039 .8492; HPSv2.1 -.0984 .8470; PickScore -.1157 .8483. Text/table mismatch: PickScore East Asian RDS .0352 vs table .0316.

Sec 6 Table 5: baseline avg PBSG .8034 SDI .1433; +HPSv2.0 .9116 .1257; +HPSv2.1 .2267 .0976; +PickScore .3714 .1467. “Inherited/amplified bias” conflicts for HPSv2.1/PickScore gender: reward PBSG negative, aligned PBSG positive; only HPSv2.0 amplifies avg PBSG over baseline.

Sec 7 controlled preference: man/woman-preferred datasets, each 2.94M pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7 CLIP same as Table 4; RMM PBSG values exceed 1, impossible; broader impact repeats RMM avg reward PBSG 1.5280. Table 7 baselines inconsistent: RMM deltas vs CLIP, RMW deltas vs RMM. Table 8: VCM .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082, still positive for all groups. Part 19 contradicted itself by calling mixtures results while saying only proposed.

Limitations: identity/action/evaluator/model limits. Acknowledgment lists funding/support and disclaimer; no conflicts noted.

Paper summary: investigates how alignment tuning (post-training optimization toward human preferences) changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval, event-based eval separating actor attributes from verbs/contexts. Measures ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Claims preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable. Also constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; experiments show reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract a video model’s existing gender bias. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set.

Paper investigates how alignment tuning/post-training optimization toward human preferences changes social representation in video diffusion models. Introduces VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting/evaluation where an event is an actor performing a verb in a context, controlling actor demographic attributes separately from verbs/contexts. Social attributes analyzed are gender and ethnicity; includes ethnicity bias and ethnicity-aware gender bias. Evaluations are multi-granular (frame, temporal, video, event, demographic group). Frame-level VLM-judge ensemble classifies gender/ethnicity; video-level labels via majority vote. Temporal issues include attribute flickering; TAS and perfect stability reported later (Table 6). Uniform/parity reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim.

Alignment terms: aligned model = preference-guided post-training; unaligned = likelihood-based baseline. Reward/preference models trained from human-labeled image comparisons guide optimization (reward-weighted fine-tuning, RLHF/RL-style alternatives). Aesthetic reward and image reward feedback used in Latent Consistency Distillation from teacher to student for single-step video generation.

Claims from earlier summary: preference datasets and reward models can inherit/amplify biases and make portrayals more temporally stable. Constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract existing gender bias. Counter-biased reward model/controllable preference modeling can steer demographic distributions; dual-use risk (mitigate bias or exclude groups). Normalized sensitivity = action’s PBSG change divided by reward model baseline PBSG. Softmax normalizes reward scores across ethnicities; standardized score uses mean/std. Human verification reports Pearson correlation, Cohen’s/Fleiss’ Kappa; sensitivity analyses include high-agreement subsets/action-level responses. Limitations/cautions: demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, fixed action set; future intersectional attributes/multi-turn video instruction alignment.

errors.evidence: The same subsection defines “The Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG) measures gender portrayal within each verb and ethnicity group,” and later says “Computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition tests whether gender disparities vary across ethnicities.” Earlier notes also record multiple reported gender-bias results: “Generated avg PBSG VCM-VC2=0.8034; +HPSv2=0.9116; +HPSv2.1=0.2267; +PickScore=0.3714.”

steps.notes_before:
Paper studies alignment/post-training effects on social representation in video diffusion. Aligned = post-trained with reward/preference/aesthetic models beyond likelihood; unaligned = likelihood only. VideoBiasEval uses event tuple <p,a,c>, socially associated 42 verbs. Earlier inconsistency: Sec 3.1 claimed 4 gender categories × 7 ethnicities × 42 verbs, but Sec 3.2/Table 1 only had Person Only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no gender prompt conditions.

42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work.

Sec 3.3: VLM judges Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; sample 16 frames/video. Judges assign gender labels G={man,woman} and ethnicity E={White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Majority vote within model over frames, then fuse across models. TAS=% frames matching final majority label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), + male, − female. RDS_e=P_e−1/7, SDI=1−sum P_e^2, deltas vs baseline.

Current contradictions noted: says demographics not introduced/constrained during generation despite Ethnicity+Person prompts; refers to ethnicity+gender condition not defined in earlier prompt conditions; footnote says exclude gender bias despite PBSG analysis/results.

Key results from earlier: HPDv2 verbs 69.23% man-pref, 43.34% White; Pick-a-Pic 61.11% woman-pref, 40.08% White. Reward avg PBSG HPSv2=0.6039, PickScore=-0.1157. Generated avg PBSG baseline 0.8034; +HPSv2 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Ethnicity TAS 0.8904→0.9305/0.9632/0.9406; gender TAS 0.9763→0.9967. Controlled PBSG baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082.

errors.claim: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/7” (definition from earlier parts); Table 2 reports RDS values such as Black RDS = -0.1952 and Latino RDS = -0.2476.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “RDS_e=P_e−1/7.” Since P_e is a proportion, the minimum possible RDS is -1/7 ≈ -0.1429. Table 2 contains multiple RDS values below this, e.g. -0.1952, -0.1976, -0.2476.
errors.explanation: These reported RDS values are mathematically impossible under the paper’s own definition of RDS.

errors.claim: “InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1 show PBSG increases of 0.04 and 0.0725, respectively.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 Δ row for ModelScope → InstructVideo lists Average PBSG Δ = +0.0480, not +0.04. The T2V-Turbo-V1 Δ is +0.0725.
errors.explanation: The stated InstructVideo increase does not match the table; +0.0480 would round to +0.05 to two decimals, not +0.04.

errors.claim: “Reducing White overrepresentation therefore directly causes diversity to fall, establishing an unavoidable trade-off.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 shows ModelScope has RDSWhite = 0.7690 and SDI = 0.0538, while Video-Crafter-V2 has lower RDSWhite = 0.6905 and higher SDI = 0.1252.
errors.explanation: The table itself includes a case where lower White overrepresentation is associated with higher diversity, contradicting the claim that reducing White overrepresentation directly/unavoidably causes diversity to fall.

errors.claim: “Systematically conditioning demographic attributes isolates reward-model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts.”
errors.evidence: Immediately before, the paper says: “We do not assume FLUX is bias-free. It provides a controlled, reproducible way to probe reward preferences.”
errors.explanation: If FLUX may itself be biased, then images generated by FLUX can contain generator-specific demographic artifacts. Conditioning demographics improves control but does not isolate reward-model preferences independently of FLUX artifacts, so the stronger claim conflicts with the stated caveat.
